findings.title: The test-fixture cache key escapes its own expression, so one immutable key is shared by every run
findings.impact: The test suite can validate against fixture content that does not correspond to the commit the workflow pins, so a run can pass or fail on the wrong corpus without anything indicating it. It is also the shape a cache-poisoning finding takes: content written into one immutable key by anyone able to run the workflow is later consumed by the build. GitHub's cache scoping keeps fork pull requests out, which is why this stays low.
findings.evidence: Line 38 reads `key: suite-\${{ env.APISGURU_COMMIT }}`. The backslash prevents interpolation, so the literal string including the braces becomes the cache key rather than the value of APISGURU_COMMIT declared at line 9. Two consequences follow directly. The key never changes when the pinned fixture commit changes, so a cache written under an older APISGURU_COMMIT is restored for a run that expects a newer one; and because there is only ever one key, the cached content is shared by every branch that can reach it rather than being partitioned per fixture revision. The cached paths are the two APIs-guru fixture directories declared at lines 36-37, which the test suite reads.

findings.title: The middleware's default logger writes the full validation error, which embeds the submitted value and the whole schema
findings.impact: Request content that failed validation - which is exactly the content most likely to be a credential typed into the wrong field, a token, or a personal identifier - lands in the application log at whatever retention and access level that log has. Anyone who can read the logs sees data they were not meant to see. Nothing is disclosed to the requester: the default errFunc writes only a generic string (middleware.go:65-67), so this is a log-side exposure only.
findings.evidence:
The default logFunc installed by NewValidator is `log.Printf("%s: %v", message, err)` (middleware.go:68-70), and Middleware calls it on every rejected request with the validation error itself (line 135) and on every unmatched route with the full request URL (line 124). What that error carries is not a summary: SchemaError.Error() appends "
Schema:
  " followed by the JSON-encoded schema and "
Value:
  " followed by the JSON-encoded offending value (openapi3/schema.go:3120-3131), unless the package-level SchemaErrorDetailsDisabled is set - and it is declared false at openapi3/schema.go:34. RequestError.Error() wraps that verbatim (openapi3filter/errors.go:23-38) and ParseError.Error() likewise carries its Value (openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:66-82). findings.title: No GitHub Action is pinned by commit SHA, three build tools are fetched at @latest, and one action is on an end-of-life major
findings.impact: Every mutable reference is a place where code this project did not review can begin executing in its CI. Combined with F-006 the payload runs beside a repository token. Pinning is the control that turns an upstream tag repoint into a no-op; today it is absent everywhere, and the @latest fetches are the sharpest instance because they cannot even be reasoned about after the fact.
findings.evidence: Seven `uses:` references across the two workflows, none pinned to a 40-character SHA: actions/setup-go@v6 (go.yml:28 and 200), actions/cache@v3 (go.yml:33), actions/checkout@v6 (go.yml:43 and 198), plus actions/checkout@v2 (shellcheck.yml:12) and ludeeus/action-shellcheck@1.1.0 (shellcheck.yml:15). A git tag is a mutable pointer, so each of these resolves to whatever commit the tag names at run time. Three further references are stronger than a tag and weaker than anything: go.yml:59 and go.yml:99 execute `go run <module>@latest`, and go.yml:202 does `go install github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/v3@latest` - `@latest` resolves to whatever version the module proxy serves at that moment, so the code that runs on the runner is chosen after the workflow was reviewed. Two of the tag pins are third-party outside this repository's control (ludeeus/action-shellcheck, incu6us/goimports-reviser

findings.title: Two regular expressions are compiled inside the per-query-key loop of the deepObject decoder
findings.impact: CPU spent on regular-expression compilation grows linearly with the number of query keys in the request, for a request that costs the attacker only bytes. It is a constant-factor amplifier on the same endpoint as F-001, not a separate class of compromise, and it grants the attacker no capability beyond making the server work harder.
findings.evidence: The loop at line 664 iterates over every key in the request's query values. Inside it, line 665 calls regexp.MustCompile on a freshly formatted pattern for each key, and line 669 calls regexp.MustCompile again on a constant pattern for each key that matched. Neither is hoisted: the first depends only on the parameter name, which is fixed for the whole call, and the second depends on nothing at all. The number of iterations is the number of distinct query keys the client sent, which is bounded only by the size of the request line that net/http accepts, so the count of compilations scales with the attacker's URL length rather than with anything about the document.

findings.title: YAML request bodies are decoded with no declared limit on alias expansion
findings.impact: If the decoder does not itself cap alias expansion, a small YAML body expands into an arbitrarily large in-memory value before any schema constraint is consulted, since decoding happens before VisitJSON. If it does cap it, there is no impact at all - which is exactly why this is reported at low confidence rather than asserted.
findings.evidence: init() registers YamlBodyDecoder for both application/yaml and application/x-yaml (lines 1344-1345), so any operation whose requestBody content names either media type will decode an attacker's YAML. The decoder is `yaml.NewDecoder(body).Decode(&value)` against github.com/oasdiff/yaml3 (import at line 22) with no decoder options, no size limit and no depth or expansion setting - the whole function is five lines. Nested-alias expansion (the billion-laughs shape) is the classic amplifier for this decoder family, and nothing in this repository bounds it: the caller passes an unbounded io.Reader and reads whatever the decoder produces into `any`.

findings.title: An array index taken verbatim from a query parameter name sizes a slice allocation (memory exhaustion)
findings.impact: One unauthenticated HTTP request of a few dozen bytes makes the server process allocate memory proportional to an integer the attacker chose. On 64-bit the practical outcome is an out-of-memory kill of the whole API process, which Go cannot recover from; under a memory-capped container it is a restart loop. The allocation happens inside request validation, so it lands before the application's handler, before any authorization check, and before any per-route quota the application implements itself.
findings.evidence: Source is the raw HTTP query string, traced rather than assumed: RequestValidationInput.GetQueryParams returns input.Request.URL.Query() (openapi3filter/validate_request_input.go:31-37), i.e. url.ParseQuery over the wire, which percent-decodes both keys and values. Two routes reach the same sink. (a) style deepObject: urlValuesDecoder.DecodeObject lines 661-687 walks every query key matching `^<param>\[`, pulls out every bracket group with FindAllStringSubmatch(key, -1), and joins them into a property path at line 679. (b) the DEFAULT style for query parameters - Parameter.SerializationMethod returns {form, explode:true} when the document sets neither (openapi3/parameter.go:293-302) - where line 650 copies EVERY query key into the property map verbatim, the parameter name not being part of the key at all in that style. Both feed makeObject (line 911), which splits the key on urlDecoderDe

findings.title: OpenAPI 3.1 validation silently falls back to a validator that enforces none of the 2020-12 keywords
findings.impact: An API author who wrote 2020-12 constraints into a 3.1 document believes those constraints gate the request; they do not. `unevaluatedProperties: false` is the 2020-12 way to refuse unexpected properties across composed schemas, so its silent absence reopens the mass-assignment surface it was written to close; `dependentRequired` and `if/then/else` silently stop coupling fields; `propertyNames` and `patternProperties` stop restricting keys. What the attacker gains is the ability to submit shapes the specification forbids - what that is worth depends on the handler behind it, which is why this is medium and not high.
findings.evidence: openapi3filter turns on the 2020-12 path for every 3.1 document (openapi3filter/validate_request.go:242-244 and 354-356 append EnableJSONSchema2020 when route.Spec.IsOpenAPI31OrLater()). Schema.VisitJSON then routes to useJSONSchema2020 (openapi3/schema.go:1945-1947). useJSONSchema2020 is three lines: build the validator, and `if err != nil { return schema.visitJSON(settings, value) }` - a silent downgrade with no error, no log and no option to make it fail closed. What the downgrade costs is checkable in this tree: grepping the whole value-validation range of schema.go (lines 1942-3000, the visitJSON/visitJSONObject/visitJSONArray/visitJSONString family) for PrefixItems, Contains, PatternProperties, PropertyNames, DependentSchemas, DependentRequired, UnevaluatedItems, UnevaluatedProperties, If, Then and Else returns nothing. Those fields exist only in the struct (schema.go:138-146), in

findings.title: The OpenAPI 3.1 schema is re-marshalled and recompiled from scratch on every validated value
findings.impact: Request-validation CPU is proportional to the size of the schema rather than to the size of the request, so a minimal request against an operation backed by a large component schema costs orders of magnitude more CPU than it costs the attacker to send. A handful of concurrent clients issuing empty-bodied requests can saturate the CPU of a service that looks, from its traffic graph, to be idle. It is availability only - nothing is read, written or bypassed.
findings.evidence: useJSONSchema2020 calls newJSONSchemaValidator(schema) on every invocation (line 205), and newJSONSchemaValidator does the whole build each time: json.Marshal of the entire schema (line 21), json.Unmarshal into a map (line 27), a full recursive transformOpenAPIToJSONSchema walk (line 32), jsonschema.NewCompiler(), AddResource and Compile (lines 35-45), the last of which recompiles every regular expression in pattern and patternProperties. There is no cache: `grep -rn 'newJSONSchemaValidator|jsonSchemaValidator'` over the module returns only the declaration, this one call site and the struct - nothing stores or reuses the result, and the compiled validator is discarded when the function returns. The call site above it is per request and per value: openapi3filter appends EnableJSONSchema2020 in ValidateParameter (validate_request.go:242) and in ValidateRequestBody (validate_request.go:354)

findings.title: Enabling external $ref resolution grants unbounded local file reads and outbound requests, with no confinement and no timeout
findings.impact: A service that parses OpenAPI documents supplied by its users - a spec linter, a gateway that ingests uploaded definitions, a converter, a CI check on a pull request - reads any file its process can read and returns the content inside the resolved document, which is typically rendered back to the submitter; and it issues arbitrary GETs from its own network position, reaching loopback services, internal hosts and cloud metadata. The all-or-nothing flag is the core of it: there is no way to allow `./common/schemas.yaml` without also allowing `/proc/self/environ` and `http://169.254.169.254/`.
findings.evidence: With Loader.IsExternalRefsAllowed set - which the README's own request-validation quick-start does at README.md:114 - a $ref string from the document becomes a filesystem path or an outbound URL with nothing in between. resolvePath (openapi3/loader.go:307-319) returns an absolute path unchanged when filepath.IsAbs, and otherwise joins it with path.Join after path.Dir, which normalises `..` and therefore walks out of the document's directory. ReadFromFile then calls os.ReadFile(path.Clean(...)) with no base-directory check (loader_uri_reader.go:79-84), and ReadFromHTTP issues a GET to whatever host the ref names (lines 51-69). The loader computes the very value that would confine this and never reads it: `grep -rn 'rootDir|rootLocation'` over the whole module - tests included - returns the two field declarations (loader.go:60-61), the two assignments (loader.go:95 and 191) and nothing els

findings.title: Neither CI workflow declares permissions, and the job token is exported to steps that fetch and run third-party code at @latest
findings.impact: If any of the three @latest toolchain modules is compromised upstream, the malicious version executes on a runner that has the repository's GITHUB_TOKEN in its environment and in .git/config. With a read+write default that is push access to the repository from CI, which is the standard route from a compromised build tool to a compromised release.
findings.evidence: Neither .github/workflows/go.yml nor .github/workflows/shellcheck.yml contains a `permissions:` key at any level, so both inherit the repository's default GITHUB_TOKEN permission, which may be read+write. go.yml additionally puts the token into the job environment at line 10 (`GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}`), which makes it visible to every step of build-and-test - including line 59, `go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/modernize/cmd/modernize@latest`, and line 99, the same shape for nilness. The sibling job check-goimports has no env block but does `go install github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/v3@latest` (line 202) and then executes it over every file (line 204) after actions/checkout@v6 (line 198); checkout persists the job token into .git/config by default, so third-party code running afterwards can read it from disk even without the env var. findings.title: A schema pattern that fails to compile leaves a nil matcher that is then called, panicking under MultiError
findings.impact: Every request that reaches that string schema panics inside validation. Under net/http the per-connection recover turns it into a dropped connection and a 500 rather than a process death, so what the attacker gains beyond an ordinary validation rejection is marginal; where the same validation runs outside an HTTP server goroutine - a worker, a batch validator, a custom transport - the panic is unrecovered and takes the process with it.
findings.evidence: Lines 2654-2666: the compiled matcher is looked up in the global cache, and when it is absent compilePattern is called. On failure the code branches on settings.multiError - `if !settings.multiError { return err }` - and when MultiError is on it appends the error and falls through to `if !cp.MatchString(value)` at line 2666 with the failed matcher. compilePattern returns that matcher unset on the error path (openapi3/schema_pattern.go:16-32): with the default compiler `cp, err = regexp.Compile(...)` assigns a nil *regexp.Regexp into the RegexMatcher interface, so the interface is non-nil, the nil check at line 2657 does not catch it, and MatchString dereferences a nil receiver; with a caller-supplied RegexCompilerFunc that returns (nil, err) the interface itself is nil and the method call panics directly. Both are unrecoverable nil dereferences. MultiError is a one-line opt-in that opena

findings.title: The zip body decoder appends the whole read buffer instead of the bytes actually read
findings.impact: Two effects, both bounded. The string handed to schema validation - and therefore to the application - contains bytes that were never in the uploaded archive, so the value validated is not the value received, which is a data-integrity defect in a component whose entire job is to decide what the value is. And an archive full of tiny entries turns each 46-byte central-directory record into 256 bytes of retained output plus 256 bytes of pre-allocated capacity, a roughly five-fold amplification on top of whatever the compression ratio already provides.
findings.evidence: Line 1637 reads into a fixed 256-byte buffer and captures the count, `n, err := rc.Read(buffer)`; line 1639 then appends the entire buffer, `content = append(content, buffer...)`, and never uses n except to decide whether to append at all. Every short read - the last read of every entry, and every read of an entry smaller than 256 bytes - therefore contributes 256 bytes, of which only n came from the archive and the rest is whatever the previous iteration left behind. The same function also sizes its output from a number the archive declares: line 1623 does `make([]byte, 0, bufferSize*len(zr.File))`, where len(zr.File) is the entry count parsed out of the central directory that arrived in the request body.

findings.title: A credential-shaped string is committed in a vendored test fixture
findings.impact: None demonstrated. The value is a public identifier inside example data from a published API description, the signature that accompanies it expired in 2017, and the secret half that would make it usable is not present. It is recorded so that the next reader does not repeat the scan and so the hit is not mistaken for an unreported live credential.
findings.evidence: A distinctive-format scan over all 1667 tracked files - the whole tree, testdata included, for AWS-style access key identifiers, GitHub personal-access-token prefixes, fine-grained PAT prefixes, Anthropic and Slack key formats, Google API keys, GitLab tokens and PEM private-key headers - returned exactly one hit, redacted here as [REDACTED:secret]. It sits inside an `examples.response.value` block of a vendored third-party OpenAPI description, as one query parameter of a pre-signed S3 URL dated 2017 with a one-hour expiry. The matched token is an access key identifier, not a secret access key; no corresponding secret and no private key material appears anywhere in the tree. A second heuristic scan for assignment-shaped credentials outside testdata returned nothing.

findings.title: The shipped middleware buffers whole request and response bodies with no cap, and reads the request body twice
findings.impact: Memory per in-flight request is a small multiple of the request body and, for the shipped middleware, of the response body as well, with no ceiling the library sets. Go's net/http imposes no default request-body limit, so an application that adopts Validator.Middleware and assumes the library validates safely inherits an unbounded buffer on both directions; streaming responses also stop streaming under strict mode. The multiplier is small and the input is proportional to what the attacker actually sends, which is what keeps this a hardening item rather than the amplification of F-001.
findings.evidence: ValidateRequestBody does `io.ReadAll(req.Body)` at line 271 with no limit and then re-seats the bytes as a new body. validateSecurityRequirement does the same thing independently at line 448, and it runs first - ValidateRequest calls the security block at lines 45-59 before the request body block at lines 91-115 - so a request that has both security requirements and a body is fully buffered twice, plus a third copy once decodeBody produces the decoded value. On the response side, Validator.Middleware wraps the writer in either strictResponseWrapper, which buffers the entire response before anything is sent (middleware.go:252-257), or warnResponseWrapper, which tees every byte into a bytes.Buffer even when strict mode is off (middleware.go:195). Neither wrapper has a cap, and neither ValidateRequest nor Middleware installs http.MaxBytesReader. A search for a declared bound found none to e

advisories_to_match.summary: kin-openapi has uncontrolled resource consumption in openapi3filter deepObject query parameter decoding
advisories_to_match.description:
### Summary

An uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability in `openapi3filter` lets any unauthenticated client force multi-gigabyte heap allocation with a single, tiny HTTP request. When a spec declares a `deepObject`-style query parameter whose schema contains an array (a normal, documented pattern), the decoder reconstructs the array by reading the **largest attacker-supplied index** and allocating one slot for every position from `0` up to that index — *before* schema validation (including `maxItems`) ever runs. A request as small as 24 bytes (`?param[items][50000000]=x`) drives heap allocation to **~6.1 GiB**, reliably triggering an OOM kill / restart loop on memory-constrained services.

### Details

The OpenAPI `style: deepObject` serialization lets clients express arrays in the query string using bracket notation, e.g. `param[items][0]=a&param[items][1]=b`. The decoder first collects these into an intermediate `map[string]any` keyed by the string of the index, then converts that sparse map into a real `[]any` in [`sliceMapToSlice`](https://github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/blob/master/openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go#L936):
